processing: Partially oxidised by withering and tossing, then fixed, rolled and dried, as with other Dancong.
harvest_season: Usually spring, as with most high-mountain Dancong.
appearance_dry: Tight, even strips of a yellow-brown colour with a fair sheen.
appearance_wet: Typically thick leaves with reddened edges, as with other tossed Dancong.
taste_profile: A clean, high orchid aroma with a mellow, brisk body and the mineral mountain character Dancong drinkers look for. It takes many steeps.

brewing.notes: Very steep-worthy, so keep early rounds short and let later ones lengthen.

vintage_note: As is usual for named Dancong, it is sold by harvest year and season, mostly fresh spring tea or tea rested a year or two after roasting. Clonal plantings exist, so ask whether the leaf comes from the old trees or from those.
description:
Xiong Di means brothers, and this Dancong takes its name from two trees rather than one. They grew in neighbouring beds at Wudong, alike in shape and leaf, with branches that crossed.

The leaves of both were picked and made together, which is unusual for a tea style built on single-tree lots. Otherwise the work is ordinary Dancong craft: withering, tossing, fixing, rolling and drying.

Expect a clear, high orchid note, a mellow body and the mountain character of Wudong. It lasts for a long session, and short early pours keep it clean.

Clonal plants now grow in the high-mountain part of Fenghuang, so the name does not by itself mean old-tree leaf. Ask about the source of the leaf and pay old-tree prices only with good reason.
history: One Chinese account traces the tea to the ancestors of a tree keeper named Wen Yanzao, who combined the leaves of the two trees and made a tea that stood out. The old tree stands at about 1050 metres in a garden at Kengxin, Lizaiping village, on Wudong. No reliable date is given. Clonal plantings have since spread through the high-mountain Fenghuang area.
